findings.claim: The Dhammapada 190-191 identifies this structure as the path to nibbana. (structure = the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna)
findings.truth: Dhammapada 190-191 is about going for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, and seeing the Four Noble Truths, the last of which is the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the cessation of suffering. The verses do not mention sila, samadhi or panna. The threefold grouping of the eight factors comes from elsewhere in the Pali Canon (for example the Culavedalla Sutta); Dhammapada 273 is the verse that praises the Eightfold Path.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.1 (prescribes Dhammapada 190-191); Access to Insight, Dhammapada ch. 14 (Buddharakkhita), verses 190-192 fetched and read

findings.claim: the Dhammapada 190-191, which names the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna as the path to nibbana. Always say: 'The Dhammapada 190-191 teaches that the Eightfold Path is the way to nibbana, structured as sila (ethics), samadhi (meditation) and panna (wisdom).'
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F1, and the sentence students are told to 'always say' is an invented paraphrase of the verse. A student who wrote it in the exam would be quoting the set text wrongly.
The Threefold Way is not stated in Dhammapada 190-191. The three items are right; the attribution is wrong and is removed.

findings.claim: [9] q: 'Which text references the Eightfold Path as the Threefold Way?' a: 'The Dhammapada, verses 190-191.'
findings.truth: The question premise is false, so the card teaches the misattribution both ways round. Rewritten to ask what 190-191 actually teach.

findings.claim: [1] 'Name the source in which the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna is described.' Key: 'Dhammapada 190-191 [1 mark].'
findings.truth: The answer key is wrong for the reason in F1. The question is re-pointed at Dhammapada 273, which does say that of all paths the Eightfold Path is the best, so the 1-mark source-naming skill is kept with a correct key.
findings.evidence: Access to Insight, Dhammapada verses 190-192 and 273

findings.claim: [5].marks: 'The Dhammapada 190-191 explicitly names the Eightfold Path as the Threefold Way to nibbana.'
findings.truth: Same misattribution inside the 12-mark model answer. The verses name the Noble Eightfold Path as the fourth of the Four Noble Truths, not as the Threefold Way.

findings.claim: Each lesson carries a question typed '2 marks - State / Give' (L1 [2], L2 [2], L3 [2], L4 [2]).
findings.truth: This board sets two five-part questions per religion, marked 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12. There is no 2-mark question. Each item is re-cut as a 1-mark 'give one' with a matching key.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2 Assessments and 4.4.1: marks allocated 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12

findings.claim: L2 [1]: 'Name the five components...' keyed '1 mark for all five listed correctly'. L3 [1]: 'Name the Three Poisons...' keyed '1 mark for all three correct'.
findings.truth: A 1-mark question on this paper takes one point. Asking for five or three items for a single mark trains the wrong exam behaviour. Both are re-cut as 'name one of...' with an any-one key.

findings.claim: All four 4-mark questions are stemmed 'Explain two contrasting Buddhist beliefs about ...' (L1 [3], L2 [3], L3 [3], L4 [3]).
findings.truth: 'Contrasting beliefs' is the thematic-studies stem, where the contrast is between religions in Britain. In the study-of-religions paper the 4-mark question asks for beliefs or teachings of the religion studied, and the divergence wanted is within Buddhism. 'Contrasting' is replaced by 'different'; the Theravada/Mahayana instruction line is kept.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1 (common and divergent views within Buddhism) vs spec 3.2.1 (contrasting beliefs in contemporary British society)

findings.claim: 'Mark schemes reward students who name the sub-tradition and use the technical Pali or Sanskrit terms.'
findings.truth: A claim about the board's mark scheme that no published document supports. Replaced with a statement about precision.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented mark-scheme or examiner claims

findings.claim: 'Examiners reward the precise Pali term and the fuller explanation'
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The advice is sound; the attribution to examiners is not.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: 'you must refer to a sacred writing or another source of religious teaching - without this your answer cannot reach the top band'
findings.truth: The source reference is required by the 6-mark question, but the lesson's own band ladder puts the top band at 5-6 marks, so a missing source costs a mark rather than the band. Changed to 'you cannot gain full marks'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the band ladder in the same lesson; spec gives no mark split for the 6-mark question

findings.claim: 'the examiner expects the key detail: a Bodhisattva has generated bodhicitta...'
findings.truth: Fabricated examiner claim. The Bodhisattva detail itself is correct.
findings.evidence: house rule: no invented examiner claims

findings.claim: The conclusion, a flashcard and the glossary all cite the Four Sights as 'recorded in Jataka 075', while the content_html correctly says the Four Sights narrative belongs to later biographical tradition (the Nidanakatha) and that the early Pali Canon tells the equivalent story of the previous Buddha Vipassi in DN 14.
findings.truth: Two defensible rulings. (a) Keep 'Jataka 075' everywhere: the board prescribes that citation for the Four Sights and may set questions on it, so a student must be able to name it; the content_html caveat then explains the scholarship honestly. (b) Drop or soften the citation because the Four Sights are not in the numbered Jataka 75 story. Recommendation: keep it - the prescribed citation is what earns the source mark - and leave the content_html paragraph as the accurate gloss. No edit made.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.1.1: 'the Four Sights: illness, old age, death, holy man (Jataka 075)'; lesson 3 content_html
findings.ruling: Leave: spec citation kept / figure unverified this session.

findings.truth: The standard transliteration is paticcasamuppada. The lessons follow the spec, which prints 'paticcasamupada', and they are consistent across all four lessons and the glossary. Left alone deliberately so the term matches the board's own wording.

findings.claim: Descriptions run over 100 characters: L2 107, L3 116, L4 112.
findings.truth: Over the house validator limit, but not a factual error. Flagged in case the validator rejects the unit on write.

findings.claim: The 12-mark mark schemes in L1 and L2 invite a 'non-religious perspective ... where relevant'.
findings.truth: Non-religious views such as atheism and humanism belong to the thematic paper, not the study-of-religions paper. The wording is hedged and the material is not wrong, so no edit; a student who adds one loses nothing but gains nothing.

summary: Lesson 4 misattributes the prescribed text: Dhammapada 190-191 is quoted six times as naming the Threefold Way of sila, samadhi and panna, which it does not - the verses are about the three refuges and the Four Noble Truths. The rest is a paper-structure problem: every lesson carries a 2-mark question, and two 1-mark questions demand three or five items, on a paper that sets only 1, 1, 4, 6 and 12.
